en: The Sūtra on the Transmigration through Existences Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Command.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was staying in Rājagṛha at the Kalandaka [Nivāsa].

In the Bamboo Grove Garden by the pond, he was together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, as well as a multitude of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, devas, and humans, all surrounding him with single-minded reverence.

At that time, the World-Honored One expounded for them the subtle Dharma of his own realization—namely, that which is good in the beginning, middle, and end; skillful in both words and meaning; pure, complete, and perfectly bright; the very characteristic of the holy life (brahmacarya).
At that time, King Bimbisāra, the lord of Magadha, went to the Bamboo Grove, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times to the right, and sat down to one side.
Then King Bimbisāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that the karma previously created by sentient beings, though long since extinguished and destroyed, manifests in its entirety at the time of death?”
Furthermore, if the essence of all phenomena is entirely empty and non-existent, how is it that the karmic retribution for actions performed does not perish?
I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion, will analyze and explain this for me.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Bimbisāra, saying:
"Great King, you should know this: it is as if a man, while in a dream during sleep, sees himself with a beautiful and upright woman of the human world, engaging in intimate union."
Once he has awakened from sleep, he recalls the beautiful woman seen in his dream. Great King, what do you think?
Is that beautiful human woman in the sleeping dream real?
The King said, "No,
World-Honored One! The World-Honored One replied:
"What do you think, Great King?

If this man, regarding the beautiful woman he saw in that dream, gives rise to thoughts of recollection and longing, unable to let go, could he be said to be a person of great learning and wise intelligence?"
The king said: "Not so! This is a fool, not a wise man."
Why is this? Because that beautiful woman of the human world seen in the dream is ultimately empty of essence and cannot be apprehended.
How could she engage in intimate union with him, such that this man would conceive feelings of love and attachment or give rise to longing remembrance?
The Buddha said: "Great King, it is so."
When foolish and ignorant ordinary people see forms with their eyes, joy arises in their minds and they immediately give rise to attachment;
having given rise to attachment, they subsequently develop longing; having developed longing, they harbor defiled craving;
because this defiled craving arises, they follow along with greed, hatred, and delusion, giving rise to various karmic actions of body, speech, and mind.

However, once these various karmas have been performed, they perish; at the time of their perishing, they do not abide depending on the eastern direction, nor do they depend on the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, or above and below. Yet, when the end of life arrives and the mental consciousness is about to cease, all the karmas one has performed manifest before one.
It is, for example, like a man who, having awakened from sleep, recalls the images of beautiful women he saw in his dream, which all appear before him in that same way.

"Great King! When the preceding consciousness has ceased and the subsequent consciousness arises, one is either born among humans, or born in the heavens, or falls into the realms of animals, hungry ghosts, or hell."
"Great King!

When the subsequent consciousness arises, it gives rise without interval to a mind of its own kind; thus, through continuous flow and transition, it clearly experiences the resultant maturation it has brought about."
"Great King!
There is no dharma whatsoever that can transmigrate from this world to the next; nevertheless, death, birth, karma, and its fruits are indeed to be found.
Great King, you should know that the cessation of the preceding consciousness is called 'death,' and the arising of the subsequent branch of consciousness is designated as 'birth.'"
"Great King!
When the preceding consciousness ceases, it has no place to which it goes; when the subsequent branch of consciousness arises, it comes from nowhere. Why is this so?"
Because their intrinsic nature is empty. Great King!

The preceding consciousness is empty of the nature of preceding consciousness; death is empty of the nature of death; karma is empty of the nature of karma; the subsequent consciousness is empty of the nature of subsequent consciousness; and birth is empty of the nature of birth. Yet, those karmic fruits have never been lost or destroyed.
"Great King!

You should know this: all sentient beings, due to delusion and ignorance, fail to realize that things do not truly exist; thus they falsely give rise to attachment and wander through the cycle of birth and death."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"All phenomena are merely provisional names, Established only in dependence upon words.
Apart from the expressive speech, The expressed cannot be found."
All are designated by their respective names to express those various phenomena;
yet within name and phenomenon, neither exists—this is the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
Because the nature of a name is empty of being a name, a name does not exist within a name.
The names of all phenomena are originally non-existent, yet one falsely uses names to designate names;
all phenomena are empty and false, arising solely from conceptual discrimination.
This discrimination itself is empty, yet one falsely discriminates within emptiness.
I say that when people in the world perceive forms with their eyes, it is all due to false conceptualization;
this is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
I say that all phenomena arise entirely dependent upon conditions.
This is called the proximate ultimate truth; the wise should contemplate it.
When the eye does not see forms and the mind likewise does not know phenomena, this is called the ultimate truth, which the foolish cannot understand.
When the World-Honored One had spoken this Dharma, King Bimbisāra, the sovereign of Magadha, received it with deep sincerity and bowed his head in reverence.
At that time, the bhikṣus, the great bodhisattvas, and the assembly of devas and humans were all filled with great joy; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Transmigration through the Various Existences Spoken by the Buddha.
